Konark

Konark Sun Temple

A 13th-century CE temple to Surya, the Sun god, built in stone as a giant chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

ASI and Mitra (ASI) say seven horses; UNESCO's short summary page says six.

Meet the temple

The surviving porch, the jagamohana (the hall in front of the sanctum), has a pidha roof (a roof of stacked stone layers). It looks like a stepped pyramid and rises in three tiers. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

The temple had a sanctum with a tall tower and a porch (jagamohana). Both stand on one high platform carved with wheels. A separate pillared hall stands in front, in the same line. ASI calls it the nata-mandira (dance hall), but some scholars think it was a bhoga-mandapa (hall of offerings). Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2,3,4]

For curious grown-ups

One detached hall, two names. ASI web page: 'nata-mandira (hall of dance)'. Behera: natamandira, adding that some scholars think it was a bhogamandapa or refectory. Mitra calls it the bhoga-mandapa but says it is 'generally believed to be a nata-mandapa (festive hall)'. Harle: the deul and jagamohana stood on a high terrace with stone wheels.

When?

c. 1238–1264 CE Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2,3,5]

How do we know?

Built in the mid-13th century CE, while King Narasimhadeva I ruled (1238–1264 CE). No exact start or finish date is known.

Dated by the builder's reign, not by a foundation inscription. ASI and UNESCO: 13th century. Behera: no exact date for start or finish. Madala Panji versions (begun 2nd or 3rd regnal year, consecrated 22nd) lack corroboration (Behera). Bahinipati et al. 2025, citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985, give consecration in 1258 CE.

In whose time?

Ganga dynasty (Narasimhadeva I) Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,4]

How do we know?

Built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Ganga dynasty.

Mitra (ASI) reports that Ganga copper-plates name Narasimhadeva as builder of a great shrine of Surya; the plates were not opened directly. Behera and Harle agree.

For which god?

Surya (the Sun god) Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,5]

How do we know?

The temple is dedicated to Surya, the Sun god.

Temple type?

Rekha deula (main tower, now fallen) Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,3]

How do we know?

The main temple, or vimana, was a rekha deula (a temple with a tall, curved tower). That tower has since fallen.

King Narasimhadeva I built the temple to worship Surya, the Sun god. Historian K.S. Behera says its devotional purpose is clear. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

K.S. Behera suggests other reasons too. He thinks building probably began after the king's victory over the rulers of Bengal around 1245 CE. The king may also have wanted a temple grander than the Jagannatha temple at Puri. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [3]

For curious grown-ups

One scholar's hedged view: Behera writes 'It is likely' (start after the 1245 victory) and 'possibly' (to surpass the Jagannatha temple). No other source seen takes a position.

  • Konark Sun Temple: about 39 m (128 ft), surviving porch
  • An adult person: about 1.7 m
  • A five-storey building: about 15 m (an assumed height, shown for scale)

About 2.6 times as tall as a five-storey building.

The main tower has fallen. Experts can only estimate how tall it was. Their estimates range from about 61 m to about 70 m (200–230 ft). Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2,4,6]

For curious grown-ups

Estimates only. Mitra (ASI): archaeologists conjecture 'in the range of 61 metres'. ASI web page: 'presumably over 68 m'. Harle: 'some 225 ft (70 m.)'. Bahinipati et al. 2025: 227 ft 8 in (about 69.4 m). Never use for size comparisons.

Stop 2 of 4

How it was built

Step 1

Builders used three kinds of stone. Most of the temple is khondalite, which ASI's Debala Mitra calls poor-quality stone. Laterite formed the hidden core of the platform and the foundations. Chlorite was used only for door frames and a few sculptures. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,6]

Step 2

The stones were probably carried long distances on rafts along rivers. Historians think simple pulleys, wooden wheels or rollers lifted them into place. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

Step 3

Iron was used too. Iron beams supported a false ceiling and the stone beams above doorways. Iron cramps and dowels held stones together. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3,6]

Step 4

According to a 2025 study that draws on earlier scholars, building took about 12 years and 10 months. The study dates the temple's consecration to 1258 CE. Historian K.S. Behera says the old written accounts of the building still need careful checking. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [3,6]

For curious grown-ups

Bahinipati et al. 2025 (citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985): about 12 years, 10 months and 14 days; consecrated 27 January 1258 CE. Behera 2005: the Baya chakada building accounts are 'set aside until a systematic study of the original text is undertaken'; Madala Panji versions (begun in the 2nd or 3rd regnal year) have no corroboration. No opened source gives 1246 CE as the start year.

Step 5

According to tradition, 1,200 craftsmen built the temple under the master craftsman Visu Maharana. Retellings disagree on how long they worked: 12 years or 16 years. In a popular legend, his 12-year-old son Dharmapada fixed the crowning pot (kalasa) on top. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [3,6]

For curious grown-ups

Tradition. Behera 2005 retells the legend with 'sixteen years'; Bahinipati et al. 2025 give 'twelve years'. Behera spells the name Visu or Vishu Maharana and says the name Dharmapada was first coined by Gopabandhu Das. Bahinipati et al. treat Dharmapada as a real person; that view is not adopted here.

Stop 3 of 4

The parts

More to spot

The whole temple was designed as a huge stone chariot for the Sun god. It has 24 carved wheels (12 pairs) and seven stone horses to pull it. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2,4,5]

For curious grown-ups

Wheels: ASI, Mitra and UNESCO agree on 24 (12 pairs). Horses: ASI and Mitra say seven; UNESCO's short summary says six.

The main tower has collapsed. Only its base, parts of its walls and niches survive, beside the standing porch. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,2,4]

Nobody knows for sure why the main tower fell. Ideas include a sinking foundation, an earthquake or lightning, or slow decay after invaders damaged the temple. Some scholars even doubt it was ever finished. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra (ASI): some blame subsidence of the foundation, others earthquake or lightning, others doubt it was completed; the 'general consensus' is gradual crumbling, begun by desecration by invaders. Behera: some scholars favour earthquake or lightning, but tradition is silent about a major earthquake; some thought it was never completed.

See 8 more

Part of the tower still stood when James Fergusson drew it in 1837 CE. Historian K.S. Behera writes that a storm brought the last piece down in October 1848 CE. By 1868 CE only a huge heap of stones remained. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra (ASI): Fergusson in 1837 estimated the standing remnant at 42.67–45.72 m; Kittoe a year later saw one corner 'to the height of 80 ft or 100 ft'; at Rajendralala Mitra's 1868 visit it was 'an enormous mass of stones'. Behera: the last fragment fell in a gale in October 1848; the temple was deserted by 1626 but still stood to a great height then. Mitra gives no single date for the final fall.

According to a local tradition, Kalapahar, a general from Bengal, damaged the temple. He did attack Odisha in 1568 CE. But historian K.S. Behera finds no reliable evidence that he ruined Konark. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [3]

For curious grown-ups

Bishan Swarup, M.M. Ganguly and Krupasindhu Mishra held that Kalapahar's removal of the top slab began the ruin (as reported by Behera). Behera: Kalapahar attacked Orissa in 1568 and desecrated the Jagannath temple, as the Madala Panji and other texts say, but these texts are silent about Konark.

UNESCO made the Sun Temple, Konarak a World Heritage Site in 1984. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [3,5]

In the early 1900s CE, the porch (jagamohana) was filled with sand to stop it from falling down. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [1,3,6]

Repair work began around 1901 CE. Sources give 1903 CE for the sand-filling and 1904 or 1905 CE for its completion. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,3,6]

For curious grown-ups

Behera: new phase of conservation from 1901; filled with sand in 1903 by order of J.A. Baurdillon; work completed in 1904. Mitra (ASI): conservation of the porch completed in 1905. Bahinipati et al.: filled in 1903 on the directive of Sir John Woodburn; completed early in 1905.

In 1998, the World Heritage Fund gave emergency money to the Archaeological Survey of India for a structural study. In February 2000, an ICOMOS expert found no immediate danger of collapse. UNESCO then asked its staff to help India seek support for a plan to remove the sand. Established: old records (inscriptions, digs, ASI/UNESCO) say so, and experts agree. [7,8]

For curious grown-ups

UNESCO and ICOMOS records of their own acts. The Bureau 'requested the Secretariat to assist the authorities in formulating a technical co-operation request' toward a sand-removal strategy.

Early European sailors called the temple the 'Black Pagoda'. They used it, and the Jagannatha temple at Puri, as landmarks on the coast. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

Art historian J.C. Harle calls Konark the last of the great Odishan temples. He adds that, as first planned, it was the largest. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [4]

Its family

Konark is one of many Sun temples built in India. Others were built at Modhera in Gujarat and Martand in Kashmir. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [3]

UNESCO calls the Sun Temple 'a magnificent testament to Kalinga architecture'. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [5]
